stages.title: Contractions

stages.title: Questions
fallbackDrills: Ready for one more round? Keep it clean, then speed up!

stages.title: Quoted Text
fallbackDrills: The coach said, "Find the rhythm, then let the speed follow."

stages.title: Number Row I
fallbackDrills: Run 1 lap, rest 2 minutes, then type 3 clean rounds at 4 or 5 words per burst.

stages.title: Number Row II
fallbackDrills: Try 6 steady lines, 7 calm breaths, 8 clean starts, 9 smooth finishes, and 10 relaxed resets.

stages.title: Hyphens
fallbackDrills: A well-timed reset can turn a rough start into a clean, high-focus round.

stages.title: Colon + Semicolon
fallbackDrills: One rule matters most: stay relaxed; speed is useful only when control stays with it.

stages.title: Parentheses
fallbackDrills: A short pause (not a full stop) can help you reset your hands without losing the flow.

stages.title: Symbols
fallbackDrills: Your goal is simple: 95% accuracy, +1 clean round, and zero panic when a mistake happens.

stages.title: Common Words
fallbackDrills: The best typing often feels boring in a good way. Your hands know where to go, so your eyes stay on the screen.

stages.title: Word Rhythm
fallbackDrills: Keep a steady pace through small words, then let longer words land without forcing them.

stages.title: Smooth Sentences
fallbackDrills: A clean sentence is built one calm keystroke at a time. Fast typing grows from repeatable motion.

stages.title: Contraction Flow
fallbackDrills: It's easier to stay smooth when you're not fighting the keyboard. Let your fingers move, then return home.

stages.title: Capital Rhythm
fallbackDrills: Monday starts fast, Tuesday feels normal, and Friday arrives before anyone expects it.

stages.title: Punctuation Mix
fallbackDrills: Focus first, speed second: if the rhythm breaks, reset, breathe, and continue without making the mistake a big deal.

stages.title: One-Minute Base
fallbackDrills: A minute of steady typing tells you more than a five-second burst. Keep your shoulders loose, watch the screen, and aim for a pace you could repeat again.

stages.title: Poe: Suspense
fallbackDrills: Edgar Allan Poe builds suspense by narrowing attention. A sound, a shadow, or a single thought can become huge when a character cannot stop thinking about it.

stages.title: Poe: The Raven
fallbackDrills: In The Raven, repetition gives the poem a pulse. The speaker keeps returning to the same question, and the repeated answer makes the room feel smaller and darker each time.

stages.title: The Scarlet Letter
fallbackDrills: The Scarlet Letter asks what happens when a community turns one mistake into a permanent identity. The story keeps returning to guilt, reputation, and the difference between public judgment and private truth.

stages.title: Moby-Dick
fallbackDrills: Moby-Dick is more than a chase at sea. Captain Ahab turns one goal into an obsession, and the crew has to live inside the consequences of a leader who cannot let go.

stages.title: Huckleberry Finn
fallbackDrills: Huckleberry Finn follows a boy who keeps noticing that the rules adults defend do not always match what feels morally right. The journey becomes a test of judgment as much as adventure.

stages.title: The Great Gatsby
fallbackDrills: The Great Gatsby explores ambition, image, and the idea that a person can rebuild the past if they try hard enough. The glitter is obvious; the cost is easier to miss.

stages.title: The Red Badge of Courage
fallbackDrills: The Red Badge of Courage focuses on fear before heroism. The young soldier wants to know what he will do under pressure, but the answer only appears when the situation becomes real.

stages.title: The Call of the Wild
fallbackDrills: The Call of the Wild follows a dog forced to adapt to a harsher world. Strength matters, but attention, instinct, and the ability to learn quickly matter just as much.

stages.title: The Awakening
fallbackDrills: The Awakening follows a woman questioning the life that other people have planned for her. The novel is interested in independence, expectation, and the cost of wanting a different path.

stages.title: Leaves of Grass
fallbackDrills: Walt Whitman's poetry often treats ordinary life as something worth noticing. Crowds, work, movement, and the body all become part of a bigger idea about identity and connection.

stages.title: Emily Dickinson
fallbackDrills: Emily Dickinson can turn a small image into a large question. A room, a bird, a pause, or a moment of silence can suddenly become a way to think about time, fear, hope, or death.

stages.title: Frederick Douglass
fallbackDrills: Frederick Douglass writes about literacy as power. Learning to read did not simply give him information; it changed what he could understand about freedom, control, and the world around him.

stages.title: The Crucible
fallbackDrills: The Crucible shows how fear can spread through a community faster than evidence. Once reputation and accusation become weapons, people start making choices based on survival instead of truth.

stages.title: Of Mice and Men
fallbackDrills: Of Mice and Men centers on friendship, work, and fragile plans for a better future. George and Lennie keep returning to the same dream because imagining it gives their difficult life a direction.

stages.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
fallbackDrills: To Kill a Mockingbird looks at justice through a child's changing perspective. As Scout learns more about the adults around her, simple ideas about fairness become more complicated.

stages.title: Fahrenheit 451
fallbackDrills: Fahrenheit 451 imagines a society where distraction is easier than reflection. The story asks what happens when people stop choosing difficult ideas because quick entertainment feels more comfortable.

stages.title: Cross-Country Morning
fallbackDrills: The first mile can feel awkward even when you're fit. Your breathing is still settling, your legs are waking up, and the goal is not to win the warm-up. The goal is to find a pace you can own.

stages.title: Game Patch Notes
fallbackDrills: A good game update changes just enough to make players rethink old habits. One weapon gets weaker, another gets useful, and suddenly everyone has to test what actually works instead of copying yesterday's strategy.

stages.title: Group Chat Timing
fallbackDrills: A group chat moves fast until someone sends a serious question. Then the typing bubbles appear, disappear, and appear again. Sometimes the most useful reply is the one that took an extra minute to think through.

stages.title: Algorithm Feed
fallbackDrills: An algorithm learns what keeps your attention, not necessarily what improves your day. If every swipe gives it more data, choosing when to stop becomes part of using the app instead of being used by it.

stages.title: Music Discovery
fallbackDrills: Finding a new song can feel random, but recommendations usually follow patterns. One track leads to another, a playlist shifts your taste, and a song you skipped last month can suddenly make sense.

stages.title: Coding Bug
fallbackDrills: The bug looked impossible until one line changed. The program was not broken everywhere; one assumption was wrong near the start, and every later result faithfully repeated that mistake.

stages.title: AI as a Tool
fallbackDrills: AI is useful when the goal is clear. Ask it to explain, compare, generate a practice set, or challenge an idea. The better the task is defined, the easier it is to judge whether the answer actually helps.

stages.title: Passkeys
fallbackDrills: A passkey replaces a password with a cryptographic credential stored on a trusted device or security key. The site verifies that credential without needing you to memorize another secret phrase.

stages.title: Space Signal
fallbackDrills: The signal appeared for eleven seconds, vanished, and returned at the same interval. Nobody called it alien. Not yet. The interesting part was simpler: something out there was repeating on purpose.

stages.title: Climate Data
fallbackDrills: One unusually hot day does not prove a climate trend, just as one cold day does not disprove one. Scientists look at patterns across years, regions, oceans, ice, air, and many different measurements.

stages.title: Study Sprint
fallbackDrills: A focused twenty-minute study sprint can beat an hour of switching between tabs. Pick one task, remove the easy distractions, and finish a clear chunk before deciding what comes next.

stages.title: Debate Prep
fallbackDrills: A strong argument does more than repeat a claim. It gives evidence, explains why that evidence matters, and takes the best opposing point seriously enough to answer it.

stages.title: Short Story: Last Bus
fallbackDrills: The bus doors closed just as Maya reached the corner. Instead of chasing it, she stopped. Across the street, a small bookstore still had its lights on, and a handwritten sign promised free hot chocolate after eight.

stages.title: Short Story: Save Point
fallbackDrills: Leo had restarted the level six times, but the seventh run felt different. He stopped rushing the opening section, saved his best move for the hard part, and reached the final room with more health than ever.

stages.title: Endurance Passage
fallbackDrills: Speed is exciting because it is easy to notice, but endurance is quieter. Real fluency means holding a useful pace while sentences get longer, punctuation changes, and attention starts to drift. The goal is not a perfect line. The goal is control that lasts.

stages.title: Personal Best
fallbackDrills: A personal best is not proof that every future session will be faster. It is proof that the skill exists. Good training makes that performance easier to repeat, even on an ordinary day when the keyboard feels less automatic.
